source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Introduction to the 1831 revised edition of Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
1831, Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley (Standard Novels series)

source.excerpt: Every thing must have a beginning, to speak in Sanchean phrase; and that beginning must be linked to something that went before. The Hindoos give the world an elephant to support it, but they make the elephant stand upon a tortoise. Invention, it must be humbly admitted, does not consist in creating out of void, but out of chaos; the materials must, in the first place, be afforded: it can give form to dark, shapeless substances, but cannot bring into being the substance itself.
trail: Mary Shelley added this line to the new introduction she wrote for the 1831 revised edition of Frankenstein, signed “London, October 15, 1831,” as transcribed at Wikisource ↗.
The identical sentence appears in the public-domain full text hosted by Project Gutenberg ↗.
Wikiquote's sourced-quotes page for Mary Shelley lists the line under “Introduction to the 1831 edition of Frankenstein,” matching the same wording, at Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: Popular quotations of this line usually drop the opening clause “it must be humbly admitted” — the sense and attribution are unchanged.
source.rightsNote: This passage comes from the introduction Mary Shelley wrote for the 1831 edition of “Frankenstein,” first published in London that year — the text has long been in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Mary Shelley
author.heading: About Mary Shelley
author.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley wrote Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1818) at just nineteen, after a ghost-story-writing challenge at Lake Geneva with Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley. She went on to write further novels and short fiction, and to edit and champion Percy Shelley’s poetry after his death, until her own death in 1851.

context.heading: The ghost-story summer behind the line
lead: Shelley wrote this introduction nine years after Frankenstein first appeared anonymously in 1818, using the new preface to finally tell readers how the story began: a ghost-story-writing challenge among herself, Lord Byron, Percy Shelley, and John Polidori during a stormy summer at Lake Geneva in 1816.

In it she also addresses a broader question about where a writer's ideas come from, arguing that invention reshapes existing material rather than conjuring something from nothing — a line now often quoted on its own, detached from the novel it introduces.
